text: Look around. Phone cases, bottle caps, keyboard keys. Most of them were made the same way.
Injection molding. Pull the machine apart, and it has two main halves: an injection unit and a clamping unit.
Plastic pellets drop from the hopper into a heated barrel.
Inside, a reciprocating screw does two jobs. It turns to mix and melt the plastic. Then it slams forward like a plunger.
The melt shoots through the nozzle, down the sprue, along the runners, and through a tiny gate into the cavity.
The clamping unit holds the two mold halves shut against that pressure.
Then comes the longest step, cooling. Water channels pull the heat out until the part is solid.
The mold opens, and ejector pins push the part free.
A typical cycle takes ten to thirty seconds. And one mold can have several cavities, so every cycle makes several parts.
Clamp. Inject. Cool. Eject. Repeat, millions of times.
